Hotel Equities is formalising its technology strategy to improve profit margins, focusing on automation and AI solutions as sector economics come under strain from inflation and labour costs.

For years, hotel companies have promised owners that strong room rates would eventually translate into healthier profits. That argument has worn thin. Ben Rafter, chief executive of Hotel Equities, told Skift that the economics of the sector are under strain, arguing that branded groups may be performing acceptably while property owners remain squeezed by inflation, labour costs and other expenses.

How this was made

Read, scored and filed before anyone asked a question.

Noah reads about 1.96 million news events a week, front pages included, and scores every one for direction and analytical markers against a standing index. This piece was written against that evidence base.

Hotel Equities is now trying to respond by formalising its technology strategy through HE Labs, a new internal effort designed to identify tools that can improve margins and help employees adopt them more quickly. According to the company, the priority is not novelty for its own sake but practical systems that reduce costs and make operations run more efficiently.

Brian Jenkins, a former management and technology consultant who is leading the initiative, has focused the early work on areas such as automating back-office accounting and using AI to improve labour scheduling. The company is also looking at robotics, although early experiments in hotel operations have not always delivered the gains operators hoped for.

The push comes as Hotel Equities has been reshaped by its merger with Springboard Hospitality, a deal that created a manager overseeing more than 250 hotels across branded, independent and lifestyle properties. Rafter became chief executive of the combined business, which has also been broadening its leadership team. Against that backdrop, Wall Street is starting to view AI as a more credible profit tool for hotels, with J.P. Morgan recently suggesting 2026 could be the first year such investments start to pay off in earnings terms.

results.author: Benjamin Rafter
results.text:
The Great Hotel Reset and the Future of Independence with Ben Rafter, CEO of Hotel Equities - Hospitality Net

Reading time: 2 minutes 2%

February 9

By Benjamin Rafter and Sloan Dean

Updated February 20

Image unavailable

#### Not Done with Sloan Dean

Photo by Not Done with Sloan Dean

## 3 key takeaways

1. A reset is coming, and it favours operators with strong commercial enginesRafter differentiates sharply between owners and operators: ownership is under pressure from high rates, debt coming due, and cash starved assets, while operators may see increased opportunity as properties change hands and require operational turnarounds. He believes winners will be those that can deliver not only operational execution but also best in class commercial services, including revenue management, content, and marketing, rather than relying on brands or OTAs to “bring the demand.”
2. Guests are moving from “brand loyalty” to “experience loyalty,” boosting soft flags and independentsHe describes a shift from travellers choosing a familiar hard brand to travellers seeking a tailored, local experience, while still valuing trust and consistency. That combination supports the rise of soft brands: independent hotels that use a major flag for distribution and credibility while selling a distinctive story. He expects a continued “explosion” of soft flags and a broader rebirth of independents as the market sorts out what is genuinely differentiated versus what is simply re labelled.
3. AI’s biggest near term impact is backend efficiency, with longer term disruption in distribution and guest interactionRafter sees AI as a change on the scale of e commerce, but argues the fastest returns will come from automating and improving hotel operations (scheduling, process work, exception handling), and reducing reliance on outsourced back office labour. Over time, he expects AI driven trip planning and booking to become a powerful equaliser for independents, as recommendations focus on fit and preferences rather than brand, and as hotels learn to “respond” correctly to AI driven discovery. He is cautious about replacing human hospitality, but believes AI should free teams to deliver better, more informed, more personalised service.
